The U.S. Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service issued a final rule updating 31 CFR part 356, which governs auctions of marketable book-entry Treasury bills, notes, and bonds.  
Most changes are technical, including revised definitions and clearer wording to align the Uniform Offering Circular with current auction terminology and an upgraded auction system, while leaving core inflation-protected security calculations unchanged.  
Treasury also removes outdated references, such as mentions of paper-form bids, a legacy CUSIP issuer reference, and a specific TreasuryDirect URL, replacing them with more flexible language.  
A key operational change is that noncompetitive customer bids must now include each customer’s name and bid amount before the noncompetitive auction close, rather than allowing a summary amount submitted in advance and details later.  
The rule is effective October 15, 2026, with certain bid-submission and results provisions taking effect when the upgraded auction system first goes live, and Treasury states the rule is neither a significant nor major regulatory action and is exempt from APA notice-and-comment requirements because it concerns government contracts.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: The Department of the Treasury issued final amendments to 31 CFR Part 356 (the Uniform Offering Circular for Treasury Bills, Notes, and Bonds) with an effective date of October 15, 2026.

The amendments modify requirements for submitting noncompetitive customer bids to require submitters to provide each individual customer's name and bid amount prior to the noncompetitive auction close, eliminating the ability to submit summary bid amounts.

The changes to 31 CFR 356.14 and 356.23 apply to auctions beginning with the first Treasury marketable securities auction conducted using Treasury's upgraded auction system, which will be communicated to market participants in advance.

The final rule is exempt from Administrative Procedure Act notice and comment requirements under 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(2) because the auction regulations relate to Treasury securities, which are contracts between Treasury and the security owner.

The amendments update terminology throughout the UOC to align with Treasury's current auction terminology, including using 'award' and 'recognize' in lieu of 'accept' and 'tender' in sections 356.20 and 356.23.
Outdated references, such as to paper bids and the former CUSIP issuer, were removed from 31 CFR Part 356.

The FDA announced four Emergency Use Authorizations (EUAs) for animal drugs to prevent or treat New World screwworm (NWS) larval infestations (myiasis).  
The authorizations cover Elanco’s CLiK Extra wound spray for prevention in several livestock and wildlife species, Zoetis’s Simparica TRIO for treatment in dogs and puppies, Bimeda’s Bimectin injection for prevention in cattle, and Sergeant’s CAPSTAR tablets for treatment and prevention in eligible dogs, cats, puppies, and kittens.  
FDA said each EUA includes specific conditions for emergency use and was issued under section 564 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.  
These actions follow the HHS Secretary’s August 18, 2025 determination and declaration that circumstances justified emergency animal-drug use because NWS posed a significant potential public health emergency with national security implications.  
The EUAs became effective on August 7, August 13, August 27, and September 3, 2026, and the full authorization texts are available through FDA channels, including online.

Sergeant's Pet Care Products LLC received an EUA on September 3, 2026, for CAPSTAR tablets for treatment and prevention in dogs, puppies, cats and kittens 2 pounds or greater and 4 weeks of age and older.

Under section 564 of the FD&C Act, FDA can authorize emergency use of unapproved medical products when there are no adequate, approved, and available alternatives for serious or life-threatening diseases.

The article presents **DiffTry (Differential Retries)**, a simple mechanism that assigns different retry limits to request classes so high-priority traffic gets more retry opportunities than low-priority traffic.  
It targets a common microservice problem where independently scaled services become temporarily miscoordinated, causing overloads, rejections, and retry storms that can be worsened by malicious low-value traffic spikes.  
Unlike centralized or overload-sensing solutions, DiffTry is designed to be lightweight, stateless, and locally enforced (e.g., via service mesh), so it can prioritize important requests without cross-service coordination or application code changes.  
The authors build analytical models for both single-service and multi-service networks, proving convergence of their iterative solution, establishing broad uniqueness conditions (especially for DAG-like service graphs), and showing monotonic gains as retry budgets increase.  
Simulations and live Kubernetes experiments closely match the theory and show that DiffTry significantly lowers high-priority rejection rates, improves high-priority throughput/goodput, and reduces the impact of incidental and adversarial overloads.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a stateless mechanism that assigns different retry-attempt limits to different priority classes of requests to achieve differentiation in rejection rates.
Under overload with DiffTry, high-priority requests achieve a rejection rate of around 15% and account for about 85% of successful completions when both classes contribute 50% of input load.
DiffTry requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination and is implemented as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application code changes.

The paper develops an analytical model for DiffTry starting with two services in tandem, then generalizes it to networks of services using an open-network model combined with flow classes and priorities.

The paper proves that network-wide class-level success rates increase monotonically with retry limits and validates the analysis on a live Kubernetes deployment where measured rejection closely matches the theoretical predictions.
DiffTry assigns different retry attempt limits to requests from different priority classes to prioritize high-value transactions during overload.

The FAA adopted a final airworthiness directive for certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes.  
The rule was prompted by reports of insufficient clearances in the right wing between fuel and hydraulic components (and related hardware), which could create an ignition source in the fuel tank during a lightning strike if not corrected.  
To fix this, operators must perform specific part replacements and clearance inspections, plus any required follow-on repairs, as detailed in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49, and the rule takes effect on November 18, 2026.  
The FAA received supportive comments and additional requests for an emergency directive or a reopened comment period, but rejected those requests and finalized the AD with only minor editorial changes.  
The agency estimates the AD affects 60 U.S.-registered aircraft, with required actions costing about $2,693 per airplane (about $161,580 total) and possible on-condition repairs costing up to $5,772 more per airplane, potentially reduced by warranty coverage.

The AD was prompted by Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 dated October 1, 2025, which reported low clearance conditions in the right wing between fuel line flexible coupling and harness support bracket clip-nut, between fuel line flexible coupling and hydraulic system, and between hydraulic system and fuel vent tube.

The effective date of FAA AD 2026-20-09 is November 18, 2026.

summary_responses.subtopic: Public Administration, Labor Policy & Family Leave
summary_responses.response:
The Office of Personnel Management issued a direct final rule updating its title 5 FMLA regulations to codify statutory changes enacted in 2021 and 2023.  
The rule broadens how employees can meet FMLA’s 12-month service requirement by counting virtually all federal civilian service, including temporary or intermittent service, plus service with USPS, the Postal Regulatory Commission, and NAFIs.  
It also newly allows certain honorable active-duty military service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, and Marine Corps to count toward that eligibility threshold, which also affects paid parental leave eligibility because PPL is substituted for FMLA leave.  
At the same time, the rule confirms that annual and sick leave provided under non-title 5 authorities may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave and removes title 5 FMLA coverage for Veterans Health Administration employees covered by 38 U.S.C. 7421.  
The rule is set to take effect on December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are submitted by November 16, 2026, in which case OPM says it will withdraw affected provisions and proceed with proposed rulemaking.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: The Office of Personnel Management is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to OPM's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations to incorporate statutory amendments from January 2021 and December 2023.
The rule is effective December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026.
The statutory changes make virtually all Federal civilian service and certain honorable active military service qualify for determining FMLA eligibility.
The rule excludes certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage.

The December 2023 amendment allows honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps to count toward the 12-month service requirement for FMLA eligibility, but does not include service in the Coast Guard or commissioned corps of the Public Health Service.
The minimum qualifying service for FMLA eligibility under title 5 is 12 months.
